comes from 100% organic shine skin pumpkin seeds (Cucurbita moschata) through mechanical partial defatting. Pulverizing the crude pumpkin protein creates a high quality plant protein concentrate. It delivers a minimum protein content of 60% with exceptional nutritional value. This certified organic plant protein offers a high mineral content and a unique amino acid profile. Gentle processing preserves the natural nutritional characteristics and mild flavor profile of Organic Unroasted Pumpkin Protein Concentrate 60. It’s ideal across organic formulations, vegan protein products, and allergen-friendly specialty applications. For formulators seeking certified organic credentials and a neutral sensory profile, it excels in protein bars, beverages, and vegan dairy alternatives. It also performs well across specialty nutrition formulations that require clean label plant protein.

comes from 100% organic Austrian Styrian pumpkin seeds (Cucurbita pepo var. styriaca). Light salting and roasting precede mechanical partial defatting of the pumpkin seeds. Further processing and milling produce a fine, olive green to brown powder. It delivers a minimum protein content of 57% with a distinctive flavor from the roasting process. Organic Roasted Pumpkin Protein Concentrate 60 offers a high mineral content and robust nutty flavor profile. It suits organic formulations from Soups and Sauces to Beverages and Baked Goods. For formulators developing premium organic products, it delivers ingredient provenance and mineral density. Its distinctive sensory character makes it a traceable, single-ingredient alternative to conventional plant proteins.

The coffee grinder was pushed to its limits efficiently grinding certain pieces of press cake and generated significant heat during the process, which could negatively influence the integrity of the protein isolation and their biological activity. Thus, for the second isolation round we have applied a cryogenic grinder Pulverisette 2 (Fritsch, Cat# 02.2000.00) with liquid nitrogen for cooling to grind the press cakes. As only rapeseed and pumpkin isolates were demonstrating a proliferation inducing activity after the first isolation, we have chosen to work with these. We show that only by applying a more thorough and cooled grinding method the isolation yielded four times higher protein concentrations than previously ( Figure 2B ). Also, the SDS gel with the same protein amounts loaded for both isolations ( Figure 2A ) shows that the fractions corresponding to the plant albumins (around MW = 12–14 kDa), are not enriched in the second isolation. The band corresponding to pumpkin Cuc ma 5 (= 2S albumin), at MW = 12 kDa ( 12 , 13 ) is much fainter in the second isolation, whereas bands corresponding to rapeseed Napins (= 2S albumins), with MW = 12.5–14.5 kDa ( 14 , 15 ), are about of the same intensity. Instead, for pumpkin, the bands at 22–25 and 35–40 kDa are much stronger in the second isolation, which do not correspond to the known pumpkin albumins. For rapeseed isolates, the smear is significantly reduced in the second isolation, probably indicating a lower protein degradation level.
